transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-19 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Chu (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (CTO), Liam Turner (Lead ML Eng), Nora Chen (SRE), Derek Shaw (Product)
Link to deck: https://app.redwood.ai/decks/ravenport-hosting.pdf

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Ravenport's p95 latency SLO, expected concurrent streaming sessions, and whether Dedicated or Private is needed for isolation. Some mis-heard terms in transcript (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" instead of "Redwood Dedicated") and a few stutters.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE. Elena will run the technical bits. Could we do quick intros and the main constraints you have?
[00:18] Maya: Hi, Maya Ortiz, CTO at Ravenport. We're building a real-time summarization/chat feature embedded in our support product. Need to hit 95th percentile latency below 400ms for 256-token responses at peak, ideally lower.
[00:30] Liam: Liam here, lead ML eng. We generate streaming tokens to the client, so p95 for each token chunk matters not just final generation.
[00:40] Elena: Got it. When you say streaming, do you mean delta-by-delta like each token or micro-batches (say 20-50 tokens per flush)?
[00:48] Liam: We flush every 60-100ms, so smaller chunks. Think low-latency streaming with many concurrent sessions — our estimate is around 800 concurrent active streams at launch, can spike to 2k during events.
[01:02] Nora: From infra, we also need to know egress topology because we might go with VPC peering if we do private deploy. SOC2 is in flight, and KMS/HSM is required for keys.
[01:12] Samir: Understood. Roughly those numbers map well to some of our Dedicated customers. p95 below 400ms for 256-token streaming is achievable but depends on model choice, quantization and how warm your KV cache is.
[01:27] Derek: Quick question — what does Redwood mean by KV cache and prefix caching? We have users who do repeated prompts with similar prefixes.
[01:36] Elena: KV cache is the key-value attention cache for autoregressive decoding; prefix caching is when we store computed embeddings/keys for repeated prefixes so subsequent requests don't recompute full context. That can drop token cost and tail latency significantly.
[01:50] Maya: That sounds promising. Our biggest worry is tail spikes — like during product launches we saw p99 rocket up.
[01:58] Samir: Right, tail behavior is where batching and multiplexer settings matter. Also fallback policies — e.g., if Dedicated capacity is saturated we can route to a slightly larger-latency but cheaper hosted variant, or to a quantized model.
[02:12] Liam: Are those automated? We don't want surprise quality regressions.
[02:16] Elena: Policies are explicit — you configure rollouts and fallbacks. For pilot we'll propose two models: a full-precision variant for SLOs and a quantized 4-bit variant for capacity overflow. We'll include quality eval pass/fail thresholds.
[02:32] [crosstalk] Maya: And encryption at rest — how do you integrate with our KMS?
[02:36] Samir: We support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for Dedicated we offer KMS integration and we can extend an HSM-backed key for enterprise plans.
[02:46] Nora: What about network latency? Our users are in EU primarily, can Redwood put capacity in eu-west1?
[02:52] Elena: Yes, region-aware routing is standard. For Dedicated we can reserve capacity in region; for Private we deploy in your VPC in the region you specify.
[03:05] Liam: Let's talk numbers. If we target p95 < 400ms end-to-end for 256-token responses with streaming flush every ~80ms, what concurrency per GPU should we expect?
[03:16] Elena: It depends on model size and batching. For a 7B open model in FP16 with good kernels, you might get ~6-10 concurrent low-latency streaming sessions per A100-equivalent GPU if you prioritize low tail. For higher concurrency you move to batching and accept slightly higher p95. With quantized 4-bit we can double or triple concurrent streams but need to validate quality.
[03:40] Liam: So for 800 concurrent streams at launch we'd need say 80-120 GPUs? That number is big.
[03:47] Samir: It scales with how many tokens/sec each session emits. If sessions are 10 tokens/sec, that's different than bursts at 50 tokens/sec. Also our KV/prefix cache can reduce per-token work if many sessions reuse prefixes.
[04:00] Maya: Our telemetry shows average 12 tokens/sec per active session, bursts to 60 tokens/sec for certain queries. We need to support bursts to 3x baseline without dropping below SLO.
[04:11] Elena: For burst tolerance we recommend a reserved baseline plus autoscaling headroom and optional burst credits. Dedicated has predictable throughput; hosted can absorb bursts but may have cross-tenant variability. Private gives you full control but requires ops resources.
[04:25] [00:04:30] Derek: Is there support for multiplexing across tokens to reduce GPU footprint?
[04:31] Elena: Yes — continuous batching and streaming-friendly kernels are part of the runtime. We tune scheduler to combine partial generation steps across streams. There's a tradeoff: larger micro-batches reduce per-token cost but can add 10s-100s ms to p95 if you wait to fill a batch.
[04:50] Liam: How do you measure p95 in these tests? Are we measuring server-side decode time or end-to-end client observed latency?
[04:58] Samir: Good question. We typically report both: server-side generation p95 and client-observed end-to-end p95 including network. For pilot we'll collect both traces and give token-level breakdowns.
[05:10] Nora: We need audit logs for every inference request for compliance — is that supported?
[05:15] Elena: Yes, audit logs with request metadata and model versions are available, retention is configurable for enterprise plans.
[05:23] Maya: Can you run a microbench for us? We can give a sample trace and keys.
[05:28] Samir: Elena will share the microbench script. We'll need anonymized traces — Liam can strip PII.
[05:33] Liam: Yep. We'll redact and provide token/sec distribution and some examples.
[05:37] [00:06:00] Elena: For the benchmark we ask for three things: a representative prompt distribution, concurrency profile (sustained vs burst), and target p95 per prompt length. We'll synthesize a 1k-user ramp test to estimate steady-state GPUs and observe tail behaviors.
[05:52] Liam: For model choices, we were thinking of an open 13B and maybe a tuned 7B. Which would you recommend?
[05:58] Elena: 13B gives better single-session throughput but higher per-token cost and longer cold start. 7B is cheaper and often sufficient if tuned. If you need aggressive p95 tail we sometimes prefer smaller model with aggressive kernel tuning and more GPUs to keep per-session latency predictable.
[06:14] Maya: And quantization — do you have production-grade 4-bit support? We've seen weird hallucination changes in the past.
[06:21] Elena: We support int8 and experimental 4-bit modes; quality is model dependent. For pilot we'll include evals with your prompt sets and set a regression threshold. We won't switch traffic to a quantized model until you accept the eval.
[06:35] [00:07:00] Derek: On the networking side, for Private we need IP allowlist and egress control; can Redwood accept private peering and run inside our VPC?
[06:44] Samir: Yes, Private supports VPC deployment and peering, and we can do a hybrid private-control plane if needed. There are some operational steps: routing, NAT/GW, and certificate setup. We'll include a checklist.
[06:57] Nora: For compliance we'll need SOC2 docs and an architecture diagram for auditors.
[07:02] Samir: We'll send SOC2, ISO statements and a skeleton architecture diagram.
[07:08] [00:07:30] Maya: About cost — can you give a rough cost estimate for Dedicated vs hosted for our profile?
[07:15] Samir: We'll provide a modeled estimate after we get the microbench results. As a rule of thumb, Dedicated committed capacity yields lower unit cost and predictable p95; hosted is easier to start but more variable and can be more expensive at scale. Private has a platform fee plus infra ops.
[07:32] Liam: One more: cold start behavior when model isn't in GPU memory for a particular prefix — what's the impact?
[07:38] Elena: Cold starts can add 200-800ms depending on model and sequence length. We mitigate with pre-warming, KV caching for common prefixes, and model pinning. If you have very spiky prefixes we can keep those in memory in Dedicated.
[07:53] Maya: Ok. For the pilot, we want to validate p95 streaming tail and a 24-hour burst window to simulated product launch traffic. Would Redwood run that with us?
[08:02] Samir: Yes — we can propose a 1-week pilot with two phases: baseline steady-state ramp and 24-hour stress/launch simulation. We'll run the microbench against a Dedicated sandbox in your region or a Private deployment depending on preference.
[08:17] Liam: If we go Dedicated for pilot, do we get a cost credit?
[08:21] Samir: Typically we offer limited pilot credits for committed pilots; we can outline terms in the pilot contract.
[08:27] Derek: How will we validate quality if you have fallback to quantized model during spikes? We need to ensure fallbacks only happen after we pass eval thresholds.
[08:35] Elena: Absolutely — fallback rules are gated by eval pass/fail and we can notify/telemetry every fallback event. Fallbacks can be synchronous or delayed per your policy.
[08:48] [00:09:00] Maya: Any gotchas you typically see when customers move from hosted to dedicated?
[08:53] Elena: Networking (VPC peering) and key management are the frequent ones. Also, capacity right-sizing — customers sometimes under- or over-estimate concurrency and need a tuning period. We recommend a conservative baseline plus step adjustments.
[09:08] Liam: On metrics — what token-level breakdowns do you provide?
[09:12] Samir: We provide per-request token count, server-side decode ms per token, queueing time, batch size, and p95/p99 histograms. You can export raw traces for deeper analysis.
[09:24] Nora: Good. For security review we'll have our security ops run through your questionnaire. Who should they contact?
[09:29] Samir: Send to security@redwood.ai and I'll cc our security lead. We'll include contact for compliance.
[09:35] [00:10:00] Elena: Practical next step — Elena will drop the microbench repo link and a benchmarking template. Samir will send pricing and pilot contract. Liam will provide anonymized traces. Nora will share compliance POC contact.
[09:52] Liam: We can get traces over by Friday.
[09:55] Samir: Great. Any other technical items?
[09:58] Derek: One last question — do you support function/tool calling and structured output in streaming? We need partial JSON emits to the client.
[10:07] Elena: We do support function-calling style structured outputs; streaming structured tokens is supported but you need to handle incomplete JSON shards client-side. We'll provide client guidance.
[10:18] Maya: Okay that's helpful.
[10:22] [00:11:00] Samir: Let's recap — we'll send: pricing+SKUs, pilot terms, SOC2 + compliance pack, microbench script, and a benchmarking template. You'll share: traces, target p95 values, and decision timeline.
[10:38] Maya: Our timeline is to decide by end of March; pilot ideally in first half of March.
[10:44] Samir: Sounds good. We'll aim to get materials to you within 48 hours.
[10:49] [00:12:00] Elena: Small note on metrics we will report during pilot: server decode p95, end-to-end p95, batch sizes, percent of requests hitting prefix cache, and fallback events.
[11:02] Liam: Can you include cost per 1k tokens for both steady-state and burst?
[11:06] Samir: Yes, we'll include modeled unit economics in the pricing doc.
[11:11] [00:13:00] [brief crosstalk]
[11:20] Nora: One last ops question — what's your error budget policy? If there's degradation and Redwood routes to a fallback, do we count that as SLO miss?
[11:28] Elena: SLO definitions are configurable; by default we count end-to-end p95 on primary variant. Fallbacks are logged and we surface them in console, but treatment can be agreed contractually.
[11:42] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone, that was useful.
[11:46] Samir: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

Meeting end
Recap/Next steps: See action items above.
